newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovakia says Czech recovery plan will hit exports.
newsitem.headline: Slovakia says Czech recovery plan will hit exports.

text.p: A Czech economic recovery plan will hurt Slovakia's exports to its neighbour, the Slovak Ministry of Economy said on Friday.
"The so-called package of economic measures will have a significant negative influence on Slovak exporters," the TASR news agency quoted deputy Economic Minister Jan Foltin as saying.
Last Wednesday the Czech cabinet unveiled a package of measures aimed at revitalising growth and eliminating budget and current account deficits.
The Czech Republic, a former federation partner in the Czechoslovak state, was Slovakia's largest single trade partner in 1996, taking 31 percent of exports and 25.4 of imports.
In the first two months of 1997 the Czechs accounted for 27.5 percent of Slovak exports and 23.2 percent of imports.

Foltin said the main obstacle for exports to the Czech Republic would be a new requirement for deposits on imports of consumer goods. Importers will be required to deposit 20 percent of the value of imported goods on an interest-free account for 180 days.
"It is clear that the Czech government has ended its liberal foreign trade approach, since for example the import deposits are a significant administrative brake on trade," Foltin said.
"This tool will have an effect equal to an import surcharge and I'd like to see what the World Trade Organisation would say about it," he added.
Neither Foltin nor other Slovak government officials were available for further comment.
Czech Industry and Trade Minister Vladimir Dlouhy estimated the import deposits would accumulate to some 24 billion crowns over the first six months.
Foltin also criticised Czechs for not informing Slovakia, its custom union partner, about the prepared measures.
On Thursday, Foltin said the Slovak government had also worked out a strategy to improve the country's trade balance.
The plan includes laws for protection against excessive imports, limiting imports of some goods that are also produced in Slovakia, and protection against subsidised imports.
But Foltin said all the measures were not against the WTO principles and were common even in developed economies.
